source: Excel Encyclopedia (14 volumes, 2026). Concept ids match Volume 12, CurioTrail Learning Specifications.

XL.CELL.ADDRESS.title: Cell addresses
XL.CELL.ADDRESS.summary: Every cell has an address: its column letter, then its row number. B3 is column B, row 3. Formulas use addresses to read values.
XL.CELL.ADDRESS.example: Price in column B, Honey on row 3 → B3
XL.CELL.ADDRESS.pitfall: Writing the row first (3B). Excel always puts the column letter first.

XL.FORMULA.ENTRY.title: Entering a formula
XL.FORMULA.ENTRY.summary: A formula starts with = and refers to cells, so it recalculates when the data changes. Without =, Excel stores your entry as text or a typed number.
XL.FORMULA.ENTRY.pitfall: Typing the answer (13) instead of a formula: it never updates.

XL.OPS.ARITH.title: Arithmetic and brackets
XL.OPS.ARITH.summary: Use + − * / and ^ with brackets to express a calculation. Brackets make Excel do one part first.
XL.OPS.ARITH.pitfall: Leaving out brackets changes the order of work.

XL.OPS.PRECEDENCE.title: Order of operations
XL.OPS.PRECEDENCE.summary: Excel works in a fixed order: brackets, negation, %, ^, then * and /, then + and −. =2+3*4 is 14, not 20.
XL.OPS.PRECEDENCE.pitfall: Reading a formula left to right as if it were a sentence.

XL.REF.RELATIVE.title: Relative references and fill-down
XL.REF.RELATIVE.summary: A reference without $ is stored as an offset. Filled down, =B2*C2 becomes =B3*C3, so one formula serves a whole column.
XL.REF.RELATIVE.pitfall: Typing a separate formula (or number) on every row.

ref.chapter: Ch. 5 · References: how formulas point at data

XL.REF.ABSOLUTE.title: Absolute references ($)
XL.REF.ABSOLUTE.summary: $ locks a reference so it doesn't move when the formula is copied. Use it for single settings every row shares, like a tax rate.
XL.REF.ABSOLUTE.example: =B2*$E$2 filled down keeps using the rate in E2
XL.REF.ABSOLUTE.pitfall: =B2*E2 filled down drifts to E3, E4… which are empty, so tax shows 0.

XL.FN.SUM.title: SUM and ranges
XL.FN.SUM.summary: A range is first:last, like D2:D5. SUM adds every number in it and keeps working when values change.
XL.FN.SUM.pitfall: A range that stops one row short, or includes the total cell itself.

XL.FN.AVERAGE.title: AVERAGE
XL.FN.AVERAGE.summary: AVERAGE adds a range and divides by how many numbers it contains. Choose the range as carefully as the function.
XL.FN.AVERAGE.pitfall: Dividing a SUM by the wrong count, or averaging the wrong column.

XL.FN.MINMAX.title: MIN and MAX
XL.FN.MINMAX.summary: MAX returns the largest number, MIN the smallest. MIN(a,b) also picks the smaller of two values — handy for 'you can't sell more than customers want'.
XL.FN.MINMAX.pitfall: Mixing them up, or pointing at the wrong column.

XL.ERR.TYPES.title: The error family
XL.ERR.TYPES.summary: #DIV/0! divides by zero or an empty cell; #NAME? doesn't recognise a word; #VALUE! does arithmetic on text; #REF! points at a deleted cell.
XL.ERR.TYPES.pitfall: Hiding errors instead of reading what they say.

XL.KPI.MARGIN.title: Profit and margin
XL.KPI.MARGIN.summary: Profit is revenue minus cost. Everything you buy is paid for, but you only earn on what sells — unsold stock is a cost.
XL.KPI.MARGIN.pitfall: Counting profit on stock nobody bought.
